awd_titl_txt: Conference: Early-Career and Student Support for the XXII Householder Symposium
awd_abstract_narration:
The Householder Symposium XXII will be held June 8-13, 2025, at the Statler Hotel on the campus of Cornell University in Ithaca, NY. The symposium gathers the world's most active researchers in numerical linear algebra once every three years to review advances in the field, present recent theoretical and practical results, and assess where the field is headed in the future. A hallmark of the Symposium is its intimate atmosphere, which promotes close personal interaction and the free exchange of ideas. Many researchers in numerical linear algebra consider this gathering to be the most important and influential meeting in the field, reflecting its rich tradition dating back to the original "Gatlinburg" conferences founded by Alston Householder in the 1960s. This proposal supports the travel costs of 12 junior U.S. researchers to the Householder Symposium XXII. The funds will provide essential support for U.S. graduate students and recent Ph.D.s who might otherwise be unable to attend. By enabling full participation for promising junior members of the U.S. numerical linear algebra community, these NSF funds ensure that early-career scientists are introduced to leading experts in the field and have opportunities to showcase their cutting-edge work. The Householder Symposium has traditionally been a gateway conference into numerical linear algebra, making the attendance of junior scientists vital both for their professional development and for maintaining the robust U.S. competitiveness in this critical discipline. 

Key topics to be emphasized at Householder XXII include the solution of large systems of linear equations, eigenvalue problems, preconditioning, perturbation theory, least squares, integral equations, and diverse applications in scientific and engineering computation, such as control, systems and signal processing, data mining, data compression, and bioengineering. Advances in numerical linear algebra have had profound effects on numerous scientific and technological fronts, including web search engines, the global positioning system, high-speed supercomputing algorithms, machine learning, and data science. Ensuring that the next generation of researchers actively participates in the conference will sustain the innovative momentum needed to address future challenges in science and engineering. More information about the conference is available at the website: https://householder-symposium.github.io.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
This award provided support for twelve early career researchers (graduate students and postdoctoral scholars) to attend the Householder Symposium XXII. The symposium was held in Ithaca, NY on the campus of Cornell University in June 2025. The award covered selected participants registration fees (which included the hotel) and travel costs.

Accordingly, the project's primary purpose of this award was professional development for early-career researchers. Although invitation-only—with invitations determined by the Householder committee from public applications—the Symposium is deliberately informal, and intermingling of early-career and established researchers is a core priority, reinforced by practices like randomized seating at meals. Holding the meeting in a remote location with capped attendance and minimal parallelism fosters a workshop-like atmosphere where sustained cross-generational interaction thrives. By design, the Symposium is a uniquely powerful venue for training and launching the careers of emerging researchers in the field.

The Householder Symposia trace back to a series of international meetings on matrix computations and linear algebra organized by Alston Householder (Director of the Mathematics Division at Oak Ridge National Laboratory and Ford Professor at the University of Tennessee) and held in Gatlinburg, Tennessee. These "Gatlinburg" conferences had a profound influence on the field. After the final Gatlinburg meeting in 1969, marking Householder's retirement, the series was renamed in his honor and has since been held triennially at varying venues.

The five-day meetings are invitation-only, but anyone—including students—may apply; selections are made by a scientific committee with rotating membership. A local organizing committee manages the specifics of the meeting. The format is intensive, with plenary talks by day, special sessions in the evenings, and an excursion on Wednesday afternoon. No proceedings are published so that participants can freely discuss work in progress (extended abstracts are circulated instead). The Symposium also hosts the award of the Householder Prize for the best PhD thesis in numerical linear algebra over the preceding three years.
